summary:
Bolu is a province of Türkiye and stands entirely under the national legal framework governing gender identity and sexual orientation across the country. No provincial law, directive or enforcement practice specific to Bolu is sourced. What a trans visitor to Bolu encounters is the national regime, which rights monitoring documents as institutionalised state action rather than residual prejudice.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The draft would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', with penalties of up to three years in prison, and would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require proof of permanent infertility, and would punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch describes the draft as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The package had not been enacted as reported, but authorities have applied its prohibitions in practice before passage.

Kaos GL's 2025 human-rights monitoring, presented at the launch of its report 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total. Of these, 299 were detention decisions: 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. The report found that hostility had become explicit state policy, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate that encouraged violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

Street-level enforcement carries a direct document risk for foreigners. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue those checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented her anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as enforcement was already being applied. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. The same police powers operate in Bolu. Any checkpoint interaction there is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation, and a mismatch between passport gender marker and appearance is an outing risk.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Placement of trans detainees follows registered sex, not gender identity. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey holds trans prisoners according to registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches of LGBT detainees, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, an absence of policy or staff training on LGBT prisoner needs, a binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints procedures that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care. A visitor seeking routine or emergency care in Bolu is entering a health system operating under these reporting rules.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement has outpaced legislation. The 11th Judicial Package remained a draft as reported, yet trans people describe being processed under its terms regardless, which means a visitor should plan for conduct rules that are applied before they are formally law. Kaos GL's framing of the period as a siege driven by instructions to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner indicates the hostility is coordinated across ministries rather than confined to individual officers.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need to Live in Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That reporting predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is relevant here as evidence of the depth of the pattern rather than as a statement of current law.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. Comparable public gatherings in a smaller province such as Bolu would attract the same national security apparatus.

Bolu has no documented record of the organised LGBTI+ public presence seen in Istanbul, Ankara or Izmir, and no Bolu-specific incident of violence against a trans person is sourced. The absence of provincial reporting should not be read as an absence of risk; monitoring capacity in Türkiye is concentrated in the larger cities, and Kaos GL notes off-record detentions that never reach formal channels.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bolu live under the same penal, civil and administrative framework as the rest of Türkiye, and are exposed to the 299 detention decisions recorded nationally in 2025, of which 43 were taken off the record and therefore outside any complaint mechanism.

Turkish citizens must carry national identity documents at all times and are subject to the same 'General Information Gathering' stops applied to visitors. The documentation taken during such stops, even where no fine is issued, feeds official records of the individual.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 affects residents directly. Hospitals may no longer record the 'other' option on medical-board reports, gender reassignment is now an enumerated reason for such reports following the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, and electronic reports are mandatory, creating durable official records that identify trans patients.

Residents held in custody are placed according to registered sex. LGBT detainees in Turkish prisons face arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement, restricted healthcare, transfers away from support networks, and complaints procedures that can expose them to further violence, according to Prison Insider's profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data.

Fifteen Turkish LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association have formally opposed the draft 11th Judicial Package. Residents accused under provisions of it, or under the existing morality-based articles, would face imprisonment of up to three years for behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, and up to four years for participating in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a police stop, detention, violent incident, refusal of care or denial of accommodation involving a trans person in Bolu province itself. The Bolu record rests on the national framework and on enforcement patterns recorded in Istanbul, Ankara and Kayseri. Whether Bolu police conduct 'General Information Gathering' stops of the type documented in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district is unresolved; the legal power exists nationwide, but its use in Bolu is not sourced.

The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of the October 2025 reporting and had not been enacted. Whether any of its provisions have since been passed, amended or withdrawn is unresolved here, as is whether conduct recorded before passage can be prosecuted under it.

The circumstances of the death of the prisoner identified as Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 are unresolved. No independent investigation outcome is sourced, and the demands for one, raised in parliament on 12 December 2025, had no recorded response in this inventory.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation restricts access to transition care in practice, as distinct from reshaping official record-keeping, is contested in the sources and unresolved here. Bolu's own hospital capacity for gender-affirming care, and the attitude of its provincial health directorate, are not sourced.
